title: Compare and Order
context: Grade 4, after the chart is understood and before numbers are built from digits. An adult sees a comparison rule. What the page is actually doing is putting two rules in a strict order, count the digits first and only then go left to right, because a child who reaches for the digits first will compare a four digit number against a five digit one and get it wrong.

writeup.why: Work out which of two numbers is more, and find the one place that decides it.
writeup.look: Two numbers stacked in one chart with their columns lined up, and a rail of number cards to sort underneath.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Compare and Order' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the places compared so far against the places in the numbers, two numbers in ink, the first climbing one column at a time as the walker steps and stopping dead the moment a pair disagrees; on the third and fourth phases it carries the cards settled in the rail against the cards on it. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The shared chart sits across the top of the working area, 880 by 300 at 190,202: seven columns 120 wide under headings 44 tall, and two rows of cells 96 tall with a gap of 20 between them, the upper number and the lower. Every digit takes its own period colour and the period bands lie behind both rows at once, so the two numbers share their periods as well as their columns. A number with fewer digits leaves its high columns ruled and empty instead of shifting right, which is the whole of the first phase. A digit count badge 92 by 52 sits at the right end of each row, its count written in ink and each digit of that row ringed as it is counted. The walker is an amber band 120 wide and the full height of both rows that stands over one column pair at a time and steps from the leftmost column rightwards; every pair it leaves behind dims to grey, and the pair it halts on holds amber while every column to the right of it greys out together and stays that way. The sign is written 64 tall in a box 96 by 96 at 76,300, level with the gap between the two rows, so it reads between them. Under the chart the rail runs 1086 by 160 at 64,540: an outlined groove with four or five slots 200 wide, and number cards 180 by 84 in ink on the paper colour, each carrying its own digit count badge in the corner and lying loose above the groove until it is dragged in. The order setting is a switch 200 by 56 at the right end of the rail reading smallest first or biggest first, and the rail draws an arrow along its length pointing the way the numbers are to grow. A card dropped into a slot that breaks the order is not sprung back; it settles, and the rail simply will not close. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across where the two numbers are set, and elsewhere a choice pad of large keys in the same rectangle: on the first two phases the three signs, greater than, less than and equals, drawn large; on the third and fourth the number cards themselves as keys, in the order they lie on the rail, so a card can be chosen without being dragged. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a digit takes the colour of its period, deep blue in the ones period, green in the thousands and vermilion in the lakhs, and rose in the millions where the international chart reaches; a digit under discussion, or the one that decides a comparison, is amber; a zero holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a place is told by its column heading and a period by its band before either is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the pair the child compared with its deciding place still lit, and the set they ordered, shown both ways.

phases.win: the sign is right and the digits were never compared
phases.does: counts the digits of each and gives the sign without reading them
phases.goal: counting digits can settle a comparison on its own
phases.says: Do not read them yet. Just count how long each one is.
phases.check: Away from the screen: one number has six digits and another has five. Which is greater, and do you need to see them?
phases.feels: you have the answer and you still have not read either number
phases.hands: Write two numbers of different lengths on paper, cover them with your hand so that only their lengths show, and ask which is bigger before either one has been read.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many digits has the top number? Second rung, the phase's: how many has the bottom one? Third rung: the digits of both numbers are covered and only their lengths are left showing. The sign keys stay open behind all three.

wrong.why: comparing from the left is a real rule, and the leftmost digits are the first thing the eye lands on.
wrong.move: picks the four digit number because its leading digit is the larger one.
wrong.screen: the empty high columns of the shorter number rule themselves in grey and both digit count badges fill, ringing each digit as they count it, so the shorter row is seen to stop one whole column short of the other. The child's choice stays in the answer slot.

wrong.why: half a rule feels like the whole rule when the answer arrives quickly enough.
wrong.move: counts the digits of one number and reads the digits of the other.
wrong.screen: both badges are filled one after the other, the second counting slowly with every digit ringed as it goes, and the two counts are set side by side under the chart with nothing else on the stage lit.

phases.screen: a four digit and a five digit number stacked in the chart
phases.soWhat: More digits always means a greater number, and nothing else needs checking.
phases.concept: More digits means a bigger number

phases.win: the deciding place lights and everything right of it greys out
phases.does: steps the walker right until a pair disagrees
phases.goal: the first place where the digits differ decides it
phases.says: Keep stepping. Stop the moment they are different.
phases.check: Two six digit numbers agree in their first three places. Which place do you look at next?
phases.feels: column after column agrees and then suddenly one does not, and it is over
phases.hands: Write two numbers of the same length one under the other with their columns lined up, and cross off the matching digits from the left with a pencil until a pair does not match.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: do these two digits match? Second rung, the phase's: which column is the walker standing on? Third rung: both numbers are cut to their first three columns and the child steps the walker across those. The sign keys stay open.

wrong.why: adding and subtracting both begin at the right, so comparing looks as though it ought to begin there too.
wrong.move: decides on the ones digit, reading the two numbers from the right.
wrong.screen: the walker runs from the left instead, one column at a time, each agreeing pair dimming as it passes; it halts at the first pair that differs and everything to the right of it, the ones digit included, greys out together. The child's answer stays in the answer slot.

wrong.why: the walker stopping has meant the answer every time, and it is easy to press stop one column early.
wrong.move: stops the walker on the first pair that agrees and gives the sign there.
wrong.screen: the walker steps back onto that pair and the two digits lift and lay one exactly over the other; then it carries on rightwards by itself until it reaches a pair that will not lie flat, and holds there.

phases.screen: two six digit numbers stacked, sharing their first digit
phases.soWhat: The first place from the left where the digits differ decides the comparison.
phases.concept: Same digit count, so compare from the left

phases.win: the rail closes with the numbers running smallest to greatest
phases.does: splits them by length, then orders each group smallest first
phases.goal: sorting by digit count first turns one long job into two short ones
phases.says: Sort them by how long they are before you read any of them.
phases.check: You have five numbers, three with five digits and two with six. Which three do you order first, and where do the other two go?
phases.feels: two piles by length, and each pile is a far easier job than the four were
phases.hands: Write four numbers of mixed lengths on four cards, deal them out face up, and have the child sort them into two piles by length before reading any of them.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many digits has each card? Second rung, the phase's: which cards are the short ones? Third rung: the long cards are lifted clear and the child orders the two short ones. The card keys stay open.

wrong.why: the leading digit has decided every comparison so far, so it looks as though it will decide these as well.
wrong.move: orders all four cards on their leading digits alone, mixing the long ones in with the short.
wrong.screen: each card's digit count badge fills in the groove, and the cards separate into two groups along the rail, the short ones together and the long ones together, without the order inside either group being touched. Nothing is lifted off the rail.

wrong.why: reading a list begins with the most important thing, and the biggest number looks like the most important thing here.
wrong.move: puts the largest card first and calls it smallest first.
wrong.screen: the arrow along the rail draws itself again from the low end to the high end while the words smallest first stay lit on the switch, and the cards already in the groove are read out along the arrow in the order they are lying.

phases.screen: four cards in the rail, two short numbers and two long ones
phases.soWhat: Split a set by digit count first, then order inside each group.

phases.win: the rail closes with the numbers running greatest to smallest
phases.does: switches the setting and rebuilds the rail the other way round
phases.goal: descending is the same order read the other way
phases.says: Same cards, other way round. Which one goes first now?
phases.check: You have put five numbers smallest first. How do you write them biggest first without comparing anything again?
phases.feels: the same four cards, read from the other end, and the job is already done
phases.hands: Take the ordered row of cards from the last activity and have the child read it aloud from the other end, then lay it out again in that new order without sorting anything a second time.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which card is the biggest? Second rung, the phase's: which end of the rail does it go to now? Third rung: two cards only are left on the rail and the child lays those two the new way. The card keys stay open and no card is taken away.

wrong.why: the last order came out of sorting, so a new order looks as though it must come out of sorting again.
wrong.move: sorts the whole set again from scratch and produces the ascending order twice over.
wrong.screen: the rail keeps the cards the child has laid and lifts the ascending order it already held into a second row above them, then walks a pointer along that old order from its far end, card by card, dropping each into the next free slot below. Both rows stay on the rail together.

wrong.why: the switch changed the rule, so the rail looks as though it has changed with it.
wrong.move: switches the setting and expects the rail to be right without a card being moved.
wrong.screen: the arrow along the rail turns round while every card stays exactly where it is, so the cards now run against the arrow; the card at each end is ringed and the rail stays open.

phases.screen: the rail holding the set the child has just put in ascending order
phases.soWhat: Descending is the ascending order turned round, not a fresh sort.

writeup.delight: The second phase, the step where the walker stops. It has been dimming pairs to grey one column at a time, and on the column where the digits differ it stops dead and holds amber; then every column to its right, all four of them, goes grey together in one movement and the sign writes itself in the box between the two rows. Every greyed digit is still perfectly readable and not one of them matters any more. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a four digit number and a five digit number sit one above the other in one shared chart, their ones standing under each other, with the shorter number's high column ruled and empty. On the second two six digit numbers are stacked the same way, sharing the digit in their highest place, and the walker is parked to the left of the chart. On the third four number cards lie loose above the rail, two short and two long, and the rail is set to smallest first. On the fourth the same four cards sit in the rail in the order the child has just put them, with the setting switch beside them. The running count at the top left is empty and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the digit count badge beside the upper number, or the walker, or the first loose card, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how long each number is. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any two numbers to compare and any set of cards to drag into either order, with the walker on or off. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on comparing pairs and on ordering sets in both directions.
voiceLines: Two numbers, one chart. Count how long each one is before you read it.
Do not read them yet. Just count how long each one is.
Keep stepping. Stop the moment they are different.
Sort them by how long they are before you read any of them.
Same cards, other way round. Which one goes first now?
Two more. Count first, read second.
Free play. Any two numbers, any cards, either order.
The walker goes again, from the left. Say stop when they differ.
One place decided it, and everything after it could be greyed out.

observations.why: One number had more digits than the other, and that settles it on its own.
observations.soWhat: Counting the digits first can finish the job without reading a single digit.
observations.observe: The comparison was finished before either number had been read.

observations.why: Those three places agreed, so none of them could decide anything.
observations.soWhat: Only the first place from the left where the digits differ decides it.
observations.observe: The walker dimmed three pairs before it stopped anywhere.

observations.why: Once a higher place has decided it, no lower place can change the answer.
observations.soWhat: The digits after the deciding place do not matter, whatever they happen to be.
observations.observe: Everything to the right of the deciding place greyed out and stayed grey.

observations.why: Every long number is greater than every short one, whatever their digits say.
observations.soWhat: Splitting a set by digit count turns one long ordering into two small ones.
observations.observe: Sorting the cards by length first left only two short jobs to do.

observations.why: It is the same order, walked the other way.
observations.soWhat: Putting a list in order once gives both orders at no extra cost.
observations.observe: Descending was the ascending rail read from the other end.

source_tool.description: Two numbers sit one above the other in a shared place value chart, with their columns aligned so the periods stand under each other. A digit count badge sits beside each, and where the counts differ the tool settles the comparison on that alone and says so. Where they match, a walker moves from the highest place rightwards, dimming each pair of digits that agree and stopping dead on the first pair that does not, which lights amber while the sign between the two numbers is written in. Everything to the right of the deciding place is greyed, because it can no longer matter. A second bay holds four or five number cards that can be dragged into a rail, with an ascending and a descending setting, and the rail refuses to close until the order is right.
source_tool.art_direction: Two numbers in one chart, a walker / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.
Drawn things, not abstract boxes: token tiles, place value charts with ruled columns, a number line with labelled ticks, digit cards that can be picked up, and lettered tiles for the Roman numerals.

A large number is always shown with its digits sitting in named places, with the period bands behind them and the commas drawn where the Indian system puts them. A bare numeral with no chart behind it is never used to teach place value.
Where tokens or blocks stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A place is told apart by its column label first and by its band colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a token or a place the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The ones period is deep blue, the thousands period is green and the lakhs period is vermilion, and those three bands are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The millions period is rose and appears only where the international chart does. A digit under discussion, or the digit that decides a comparison, is amber. A zero holding an empty place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a period is told apart by its band and its label before its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: The walker goes again, from the left. Say stop when they differ.
voice.onNext: Two more. Count first, read second.
voice.opening: Two numbers, one chart. Count how long each one is before you read it.
voice.onFinish: One place decided it, and everything after it could be greyed out.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any two numbers, any cards, either order.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: More digits means a bigger number
Same digit count, so compare from the left

placement.where: After two numbers have been compared on paper and the class has disagreed about which is greater. The tool shows which place decided it, which a written answer never does.

answer_key.rule: Count the digits first. The number with more digits is greater and nothing else needs checking. If the counts match, compare from the highest place rightwards and stop at the first place where the digits differ; that place decides it and nothing to its right matters. Ascending order runs from smallest to greatest and descending is the same list turned round.
answer_key.wrong: The walker runs again from the highest place, one column at a time, with each agreeing pair dimming as it passes. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Count the digits in each. One has four and the other has five.
A five digit number is greater than any four digit number.
So 39,526 is greater, and the digits themselves never mattered.
items.answer: 39,526, and no digits had to be compared
items.question: Which is greater, 8424 or 39,526?
items.checkpoint: Counting the digits can finish a comparison on its own.
items.misconception: Comparing the leading digits and choosing 8424 because eight beats three.

steps: Both have six digits, so start at the highest place.
The lakhs digits are both nine, so move one place to the right.
The ten thousands are three against one, so the first number is greater.
items.question: Which is greater, 9,38,769 or 9,17,654?
items.checkpoint: The first place where the digits differ decides it.
items.misconception: Reading from the right instead of the left and deciding on the ones digit.

steps: Split them by digit count. Two have five digits and two have six.
Order the five digit pair first: 23,651 is less than 63,215.
Both six digit numbers are greater, and 4,02,365 is less than 5,23,691.
items.question: Put 63,215 and 4,02,365 and 23,651 and 5,23,691 in ascending order.
items.checkpoint: Sorting by length first turns one long problem into two short ones.
items.misconception: Mixing the five and six digit numbers and ordering on the leading digit alone.

steps: All four have six digits, so compare the lakhs digits.
They are two, five, seven and four, and all four are different.
Descending means greatest first, so run the lakhs digits from seven down to two.
items.question: Write 2,36,589 and 5,69,874 and 7,41,230 and 4,41,296 in descending order.
items.checkpoint: When the highest place differs in every number, one comparison orders them all.
items.misconception: Producing the ascending order and labelling it descending.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Which is greater, 50,361 or 1,60,972?
items.final_answer: 1,60,972, because it has six digits and the other has five

items.question: One number has five digits and another has four. Can the four digit one ever be greater?
items.final_answer: No. More digits always means a greater number

items.question: Compare 96321 and 75632 using the correct sign.
Compare 992364 and 993695 using the correct sign.
Write 65,781 and 20,549 and 19,680 and 54,187 in ascending order.
Write 3,96,452 and 2,09,586 and 8,17,492 and 6,18,045 in ascending order.
Write 23,658 and 78,965 and 63,254 and 78,966 in descending order.
Five salaries are 2,35,000 and 1,79,800 and 1,00,000 and 2,35,185 and 1,97,750. Put them in increasing order.

teaching_notes: Insist on counting the digits before anything else, every single time, until it is automatic. Half of all comparing at this age is finished by counting, and the child who skips it is the child who says 8424 is more than 39,526. Use the step control rather than the walk control for the first few pairs, so the dimming can be watched place by place. The greying out to the right of the deciding place is worth naming out loud: those digits cannot matter any more, whatever they are. In the ordering bay, ask them to find the smallest and the largest first, because what is left in the middle is a shorter job.
generation_prompt: Build a comparison tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. Two numbers sit stacked in one shared ruled place value chart with columns aligned and period bands behind them. A digit count badge sits beside each number, and where the counts differ the tool resolves the comparison on that alone. Where the counts match, a walker advances from the highest place rightwards, dimming each pair of digits that agree and halting on the first pair that differs, which highlights in amber while everything to its right greys out. A step control advances the walker one place at a time. A sign control writes the greater than, less than or equals sign between the two numbers. Beneath, a rail holds four or five draggable number cards with an ascending and descending setting, and the rail refuses to close until the order is correct. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Set two numbers into the chart and count their digits. If the counts match, step across from the left until the digits differ, and write the sign. Then drag the cards in the rail into order, smallest first and then the other way.
